fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: Robotics LAB enquiry or an introduction through KAR/ROBOTWORLD; no personal connection verified.

fields.What they build: Develops Ballie, a wheeled home companion combining cameras, conversational AI, and connected-home control. Announced an increase to 35% of Rainbow Robotics in December 2024 and plans to combine AI with Rainbow hardware for humanoids and manufacturing/logistics automation. Ballie commercial availability is unknown; an announced launch target is not proof of shipment.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: Samsung robotics research outreach or a KAR introduction. No student partnership verified.

fields.What they build: Presented CLOiD, a wheeled two-arm home robot, at CES 2026 and introduced AXIUM robot actuators. CLOiD combines a vision-language model (interprets images and instructions) with a vision-language-action model (turns those inputs into actions); individual model names and open weights are unknown. The opened source demonstrates a product direction, not verified retail availability.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: LG robotics or university-relations enquiry, with KAR as a possible introduction.

fields.What they build: Makes collaborative robot arms and automation solutions. P3020 is a five-axis palletizing arm that moves boxes onto pallets, with 30 kg payload and 2,030 mm reach. Its public doosan-robot2 ROS 2 packages expose robot control and simulation integration; open software does not mean open robot hardware.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: sales.robotics@doosan.com or the official ROS 2 repository issue tracker for a specific technical question.

fields.What they build: KAIST spin-out building robot platforms. RB-Y1 combines two seven-joint arms with a wheeled base for manipulation, teleoperation, and whole-body-control research. Provides Python/C++ SDK and simulation assets. Samsung announced its 35% stake and subsidiary consolidation in December 2024; this does not make the hardware open source.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: official RB-Y1 support channel or an SDK issue/discussion, backed by a concrete reproducible demo.

fields.What they build: Builds DYNAMIXEL smart actuators and open research platforms: TurtleBot3, OMX entry-level arms, OMY manipulators, AI Worker mobile manipulators, and AI Sapiens humanoids. Physical AI Tools links ROS 2 robot control to LeRobot demonstration datasets and policy training. This is the strongest direct software bridge to 42AI in the shortlist; actual landed hardware prices remain unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown personal connection; public route: ROBOTIS Discourse forum and a useful Physical AI Tools GitHub issue/PR, then its global contact form.

fields.What they build: Korean wearable/humanoid startup. Sells WIM walking-assistance devices and develops ALLEX upper-body humanoid hardware for compliant, dexterous manipulation. Announced KRW 95 billion Series B in May 2026. Its BSD-licensed ALLEX simulation model is public; the repository calls physical hardware research-prototype v2 with limited research-edition access planned later in 2026, not a mass-market robot.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: official contact form, ALLEX model repository, or an introduction via investor FuturePlay.

fields.What they build: NAVER research organization building ARC cloud robotics: cloud-side robot management, localization, and a web operating layer. Builds and tests Rookie delivery robots and AMBIDEX dual-arm manipulation, connecting a heterogeneous robot fleet in NAVER 1784. An April 2025 official account reports about 100 robots and over 60,000 deliveries; these are company-reported historical figures.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: NAVER LABS research enquiry or public conference speakers; no existing 42AI connection verified.

fields.What they build: University with multiple robotics groups. Its DRCD Lab builds HOUND quadrupeds with custom drivetrains and learned locomotion; HOUND 1 used a reinforcement-learning controller for its 2023 speed demonstration. HOUND 2 is a newer lab platform, but its official page gives conflicting mass figures. This row represents the university; the lab is a contact route, not a duplicate organization.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: DRCD lab contact at its official KAIST site, or a specific corresponding author with a reproducible research question.

nodes.name: Korea Institute of Robotics & Technology Convergence (KIRO)

fields.What they build: Government-backed specialised robotics research institute (founded 2005 as Pohang Intelligent Robot Institute, reorganised as KIRO in 2012) located on the POSTECH campus in Pohang. Develops underwater/construction, medical-service, safety and agricultural robots and runs demonstration centres (safety-robot and agricultural-robot test centres) plus training programmes for industry. Specific current platforms and 2026 activity are unknown: the official site kiro.re.kr was unreachable during verification.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: KIRO international contact or RoTIC education enquiry. No Paris exchange or free training eligibility verified.

nodes.name: Korea Association of AI Robot Industry (KAR)

fields.What they build: Industry association connecting Korean government, companies, and academia. Coordinates industry networking and is a ROBOTWORLD organizer; does not itself have a verified named robot or AI model. The English home page now uses Korea Association of AI Robot Industry, while the page title retains the earlier Korea Association of Robot Industry wording.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: KAR international-relations enquiry or ROBOTWORLD secretariat (info@robotworld.or.kr). No warm introduction exists in the evidence.

fields.What they build: Korean robotics trade exhibition covering manufacturers, service robots, components, software, and integration. The official 2026 dates are November 4-7 at KINTEX, so that edition has already ended as of this research on November 13. Organizer-page participation counts conflict and are not treated as verified 2026 totals. No named robot or AI model is built by the event.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: info@robotworld.or.kr for post-event exhibitor introductions or a future student delegation. Next edition dates unknown.

fields.What they build: Deep-tech venture investor providing early-stage funding and company-building support. Its official portfolio includes WIRobotics; WIRobotics also names FuturePlay among its May 2026 Series B investors. It invests in robotics companies rather than building or operating a verified named robot itself. The investor own financing stage is unknown, so Size / stage is left null.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: communication@futureplay.co with a specific portfolio-company introduction or deep-tech speaker request.

fields.What they build: Korean online robotics community with public ROS teaching repositories and the iTurtle miniature robot project, explicitly based on TurtleBot3. The cited iTurtle repository documents the Pangyo chapter and links the Naver community. Evidence for these projects is historical; community activity and maintainership in 2026 are unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public route: linked OROCA Naver cafe or GitHub issues, first checking whether maintainers are active and whether English outreach is welcome.

fields.What they build: Seoul startup rooted in Seoul National University AI research. Co-developed CLIP-RT, a one-billion-parameter vision-language-action model (camera images and instructions to robot motions), with public code and checkpoints. In 2026 presented HABILIS Brain 0 and a stack for data, training, deployment, and robot operations. Funding stage is unknown; an investment target is not a completed round.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown personal connection; public route: partnerships@tommoro.ai or the CLIP-RT repository with a reproducible evaluation question.
fields.Sources: https://tommoro.ai/; https://tommoro.ai/about; https://tommoro.ai/contact; https://www.snu.ac.kr/snunow/press?bbsidx=154981&md=v; https://clip-rt.github.io/; https://github.com/clip-rt/clip-rt; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25558

fields.What they build: Provides GPU and Jetson computing plus the Isaac robotics stack. Isaac Sim simulates robots and sensors; Isaac Lab adds workflows for training robot policies, including reinforcement learning (learning through trial and reward).
Develops the Optimus general-purpose humanoid program and AI for perception and robot control. Public program descriptions are not proof of unsupervised commercial deployment.

Builds and operates warehouse automation, including Proteus mobile robots, Sparrow picking arms and the tactile Vulcan system. Amazon's own fulfillment network provides a concrete customer and integration environment, unlike a staged home demo.

Builds Spot for mobile inspection, Stretch for warehouse case handling, and Atlas for industrial humanoid work. These are different products and should not be treated as one general-purpose deployment.
Builds robot-assisted surgical and bronchoscopy systems, including da Vinci. These assist trained clinical teams; they are not autonomous surgeons or appropriate beginner hardware.

Builds Figure humanoids and Helix embodied AI. Its homepage presents Figure 03 for home assistance. In September 2025 it announced more than $1B of committed Series C capital at a $39B post-money valuation; committed funding is not revenue or evidence of deployment scale.

Develops generalist robot policies in the pi family. A vision-language-action model turns camera images and instructions into robot actions. Its site provides pi0 code/weight releases and later models; Axios reported a $600M round in November 2025, but the opened article did not label its series.

Develops Skild Brain, a robot-control model intended to work across different robot bodies. Its January 2026 announcement reports $1.4B raised at a valuation above $14B; claims that it can control any robot remain company claims, not independently established guarantees.

Builds Digit humanoids and Arc fleet software for industrial automation. Its September 2025 NVIDIA collaboration page confirms Series C investment and use of Isaac Lab for sim-to-real robot learning; its homepage identifies Salem as Digit's assembly location.

Builds Apollo humanoids for manufacturing and logistics. February 2026's company release reports more than $935M in total Series A financing and partnerships with Mercedes-Benz, GXO, Jabil and Google DeepMind. Apollo 2 is already in the pilot robot/model file and is not recreated here.

fields.City: San Carlos, California (current about page); Palo Alto HQ announced in 2025
fields.What they build: Develops NEO home humanoids. Norwegian origins do not exclude it: a July 2025 announcement established a US global HQ, while the current about page says San Carlos. Its last opened explicitly labeled financing is a $100M Series B announcement in January 2024, not a verified latest round.

Builds Field Foundation Models: robot-control software designed to account for uncertainty and physical constraints in unstructured environments. Its August 2025 release reports $405M across two rounds and industrial deployments; Series B labeling comes from an opened secondary funding table.

Connects university researchers and industry around domestic, medical, field and workplace robotics. Stanford's Mobile ALOHA project demonstrates learning mobile two-arm tasks from human demonstrations; the center itself also releases OpenSAI.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; public Mobile ALOHA project and center seminars are cold outreach routes, not warm introductions

fields.What they build: UC Berkeley's AI research community includes robot learning. Berkeley's HIL-SERL uses demonstrations, a learned success classifier and human interventions to improve manipulation policies through reinforcement learning. The earlier SERL project is explicitly deprecated in favor of HIL-SERL.

University robotics institute spanning robotics research and education. Its homepage describes the Robotics Innovation Center in Pittsburgh. Specific robot/model attribution was not established from the opened institute page and is left unknown rather than inferred from unrelated projects.

Toyota's US research organization studies mobile manipulation, human-robot interfaces and data collection for useful tasks. It leads core development of Drake, a tool for simulating dynamics and designing robot controllers. Parent Toyota is Japanese; this row is the US institute, not Toyota globally.

University represented here as the School type, with robotics research in CSAIL. Its Robot Locomotion Group originated Drake; core development is now led by TRI, so attributing Drake solely to MIT would be misleading.

Independent robotics hub supporting commercialization, with startup workspace, prototyping, testing and connections among startups, academia and industry. It does not itself imply a named production robot or AI model.

US nonprofit robotics industry association connecting companies, universities and investors. Its 2026 prospectus documents meetups, investor summits and hackathons, including the 2025 LeRobot Global Hackathon.
fields.Warm contact path: unknown; prospectus lists managing director Andra Keay as a public contact, not a warm introduction

geo.place: San Francisco Bay Area, California, United States

fields.What they build: US nonprofit steward of open robotics software under the Open Robotics brand. OSRA provides governance and community participation for ROS, Gazebo and Open-RMF. OSRF is distinct from the commercial subsidiaries acquired by Intrinsic in 2022; ROS 2 already exists in the pilots.

Deep-tech investor whose opened portfolio and 2025 report include Physical Intelligence, Anduril and Auris Health. Provides capital and company-building support rather than a lab-owned robot platform.

Deep-tech venture firm with documented investment in Agility Robotics since 2020 and a portfolio page discussing warehouse humanoids. Its robotics relevance is grounded in an opened investment page, not a claim to be the most active investor by deal count.

The 2026 US edition of the international robot-learning conference, November 9–12 in Austin. Combines research papers, demonstrations and workshops at the intersection of machine learning and robotics; this row is the US edition, not a permanently US-based organization.

US robotics and automation trade show connecting component vendors, integrators and customers. The opened homepage has rolled forward to May 10–13, 2027 in Las Vegas and links a 2026 recap; no claim is made that the 2026 edition was in Las Vegas.

Boston engineering-focused robotics event. The opened 2026 page lists speakers from Open Robotics, PickNik, Universal Robots and other builders, making it useful for systems engineering beyond foundation-model headlines.
Visual SLAM and camera-based positioning for mobile robots and manual fleets. Acquired by ABB in January 2024; now an ABB business unit.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official public contact to propose a student engineering talk on perception, data or control, sharing a 42AI LeRobot/SO-101 demo first.

fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official public contact to propose a student engineering talk on perception, data or control, sharing a 42AI LeRobot/SO-101 demo first.

fields.What they build: Scewo BRO and GO powered wheelchairs address assisted mobility, including stair-climbing configurations. Assistive mechatronics rather than a general-purpose autonomous robot. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official public contact to propose a student engineering talk on robot design, sharing a 42AI LeRobot/SO-101 demo first.

fields.What they build: Growing soft robot platform inspects and works in confined spaces, with modular tools for piping, cable installation and search/rescue access. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official public contact to propose a student engineering talk on robot design, sharing a 42AI LeRobot/SO-101 demo first.

fields.What they build: Neuromorphic event-vision systems provide low-latency, high-dynamic-range perception. Official address: Thurgauerstrasse 60, Zurich. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official public contact to propose a student engineering talk on perception, data or control, sharing a 42AI LeRobot/SO-101 demo first.

fields.What they build: Physical-AI data platform: LightlyStudio for curation, annotation and evaluation; LightlyTrain for training computer-vision models. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official public contact to propose a student engineering talk on perception, data or control, sharing a 42AI LeRobot/SO-101 demo first.

fields.What they build: Purpose-built robots clean fixtures and surfaces in facilities using tool changes, physical contact, learning and human-in-the-loop teleoperation. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official public contact to propose a student engineering talk on perception, data or control, sharing a 42AI LeRobot/SO-101 demo first.

fields.What they build: Autonomous mobile systems, navigation, sensing and field/service robots; its spin-off directory documents Ascento, RoBoa, Sevensense, Tethys, Voliro and Wingtra.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Stelian Coros's group combines simulation, algorithms and data for robot design, motion planning/control and learning skills from people.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Robert Katzschmann's lab studies soft and bio-inspired robots. Its October 2026 news describes a robotic hand learning finger-based locomotion in simulation.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

nodes.name: University of Zurich Robotics and Perception Group (RPG)

fields.What they build: Davide Scaramuzza's group studies autonomous navigation with onboard cameras and computing, especially micro-drones, event vision and learned flight.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

nodes.name: ETH Zurich Computer Vision and Geometry Group (CVG)

fields.What they build: Geometric computer vision, 3D reconstruction, visual localization, mapping, planning and scene understanding for robotics.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

nodes.name: ETH Zurich Institute for Dynamic Systems and Control (IDSC)

fields.What they build: Control research includes iterative learning applied to quadrocopters: estimate tracking error, update inputs and improve repeated maneuvers. Cited project is an archive, not a claim of a new 2026 result.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Bradley Nelson's robotics group investigates robots across scales, including medical micro-robotics. Listed as an active IRIS member laboratory.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Joint ETH/UZH translational accelerator in robotics, regenerative medicine and bionics/medical devices; robotics portfolio includes Tethys, Voliro and Wingtra.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Interdisciplinary AI center whose robotics core covers manipulation, locomotion, reinforcement learning, soft robots, perception and safety.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

nodes.name: ETH Zurich RobotX Center for Robotics

fields.What they build: Coordinates robotics research and community activities, including focus-project rollout and embodied-AI events. Organized Swiss Robotics Day 2026; its 2026 summer school took place in Geneva, not Zurich.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Applied robotics, automation, drive engineering, control and biomedical engineering; teaches systems engineering with robotics/mechatronics specialization and industry-linked projects.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public lab/center contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Technical university anchoring the Zurich robotics ecosystem through independent laboratories, engineering education, focus projects and student fabrication support. Labs are separate contact targets, not separate universities.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public school international or robotics program contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: University hosting the Robotics and Perception Group and co-hosting Wyss Zurich; a route into robotics/computer vision and translational research rather than a robot vendor.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public school international or robotics program contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Applied engineering education with robotics/mechatronics specialization through IMS and industrial research projects.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm contact. Send the public school international or robotics program contact a short student-project proposal and ask for one relevant PhD/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Student-led robotics community builds its own humanoid hardware and software; holds hackathons, speaker events and collaborations. The site describes its work as open source.
fields.Warm contact path: Approach the public club contact with a 42AI SO-101 demo; propose a joint student build session or remote technical exchange. Shared Hugging Face/LeRobot interests are an introduction topic, not an established introduction.

fields.What they build: Makerspace and project-support community for extracurricular ETH student prototypes, with fabrication/electronics facilities, coaching and workshops. External 42AI access is not automatic.
fields.Warm contact path: Ask the public SPH team about a hosted student-team visit; ETH-only access rules require a host.

fields.What they build: Hackerspace collective at Neue Hard 12, including MechArtLab/SGMK, CCCZH, Hackteria and other groups. Advertises Tuesday open electronics laboratory and community meetings.
fields.Warm contact path: Public mailing list bitwascherei@chaostreff.ch and open electronics evenings; check current visitor policy before travel.

fields.What they build: Academic Motorsports Association Zurich builds electric and autonomous Formula Student cars; driverless work combines perception, planning and controls.
fields.Warm contact path: info@amzracing.ch; propose a peer exchange on autonomous racing and software integration.

fields.What they build: Student-led team develops Hyperloop transport pod prototypes with custom propulsion, electronics, sensing and control. Robotics-adjacent autonomous mobility, not a general-purpose robot.
fields.Warm contact path: Public team contact; propose a joint controls/embedded project review.

fields.What they build: Academic Space Initiative Switzerland builds student space and exploration systems. NAUTILUS develops underwater gliders for polar research; ASTERIA works on rockets with guided recovery.
fields.Warm contact path: Ask the public ARIS contact for the NAUTILUS team and a student control/sensing exchange.

fields.What they build: Robotics hacker house/residency advertised for October–December 2026: builders live and work together on physical-AI projects. Site advertises shared hardware, compute and public demo events; access is selective.
fields.Warm contact path: Public residency/partner contact; ask about visitor demo events or a remote exchange, not automatic residency admission.

fields.What they build: Innovation campus and shared workshop/prototyping community at Dübendorf airfield, supporting robotics, autonomous mobility and drones. Hosts projects including AMZ/ForzaETH and industrial startups.
fields.Warm contact path: zurich@switzerland-innovation.com; request a public event visit and one relevant tenant/student-team introduction.

fields.What they build: Early-stage Swiss venture investor, formerly Wingman Ventures (renamed in 2024). Robotics/industrial portfolio includes Wingtra; not a second separate fund row for Wingman.
fields.Warm contact path: Public fund contact or student robotics event; request a short commercialization talk rather than investment for a student club.

fields.What they build: Corporate venture investor with a Zurich office; partner Alexander Schlaepfer explicitly focuses on robotics, machine vision, digital twins and AgTech.
fields.Warm contact path: Public Zurich team page for Alexander Schlaepfer; propose a student robotics commercialization discussion.

fields.What they build: 2026 national robotics meeting held 13 November at StageOne Zurich, organized by ETH RobotX with Swiss Robotics Association support; research, exhibitors, workshops and networking.
fields.Warm contact path: Public organizer contact for a future edition's student tickets/demo criteria; 2026 page says sold out, so do not recommend walk-in access.

nodes.name: Robotics and AI Hackathon — The Gallery Zurich

fields.What they build: Swiss AI Weeks event listed for 3 October 2026 at The Gallery, Thurgauerstrasse 119: free one-day robotics/AI sprint, teams up to four. Recurrence is unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: Contact event organizers about future opportunities or introductions; cited 2026 event is not an open future registration promise.

fields.What they build: Global open-source drone flight-control community hosted by Dronecode, not a Zurich-headquartered foundation. Dronecode documents PX4/Pixhawk origins and contributor/company links in Zurich; current community offers public development calls and contributions.
fields.Warm contact path: Join public Discord/Discourse and weekly developer calls; start with simulator issues or documentation contributions.

fields.What they build: Flinkbot and Flinkbot mini provide drop-in robotic handling for logistics: singulation, loading/unloading and picking. Co-founded by ETH CRL researchers; motion planning and vision are central.
fields.Warm contact path: hi@flink.so; send a small arm manipulation demo and ask for a robotics-learning engineering talk.

fields.What they build: Develops magnetic navigation and ultra-flexible devices for remote endovascular robotic interventions, initially targeting stroke treatment. Development claims do not imply clinical approval.
fields.Warm contact path: info@nanoflexrobotics.com; ask for an educational telerobotics/safety talk, not patient or clinical-system access.

fields.What they build: TINAMU RMS robotic monitoring uses automated indoor drones, computer vision and cloud analytics to measure inventories without GNSS. Also supplies a LiDAR monitoring kit.
fields.Warm contact path: info@tinamu-labs.com; propose an indoor-navigation or 3D inventory-analysis student seminar.

fields.What they build: Automated manufacturing systems combine large-scale additive manufacturing, CNC machining and inspection for large parts; company-issued February 2025 release reports a $6.7M seed round. Registered address in Bäretswil, canton Zurich.
fields.Warm contact path: Public company contact; request a manufacturing automation talk or advice on designing student robot parts.

fields.What they build: Entertainment robotics team develops expressive characters with reinforcement learning and simulation. Zurich team provenance is documented by IEEE Spectrum; Disney's 2025 BDX account describes sim-trained balancing robots. Do not equate every Disney Research Studios animation project with robotics.
fields.Warm contact path: Public research contact or Swiss Robotics Day talk route to Moritz Bächer's group; ask for a paper discussion, not proprietary platform access.

fields.What they build: Studies human sensory-motor control, mechatronic machines and human-machine interaction, especially rehabilitation and sports; develops cooperative rehabilitation technology.
fields.Warm contact path: Public lab contact with a short rehabilitation HRI/safety reading-group proposal; no patient experiments requested.

fields.What they build: ETH incubation/funding program helps eligible students and researchers convert research into spin-offs through funding, coaching and infrastructure. ETH Foundation documents robotics alumni including ANYbotics and Tethys; not a general student-association grant.
fields.Warm contact path: Ask program staff for a robotics alumni speaker; 42AI members without ETH affiliation should not assume eligibility.

fields.What they build: Philanthropic Swiss science-to-startup support initiative operated by Venturelab, with Schlieren and Lausanne contacts. Its portfolio documents autonomous underwater robotics company Tethys.
fields.Warm contact path: info@venturekick.ch; ask for a robotics founder introduction or public entrepreneurship session rather than an association grant.

fields.What they build: Student-run entrepreneurship club offering speakers, startup networking and programs including InCube and Boost. General ecosystem connector, not a dedicated robotics lab or another name for ETH Robotics Club.
fields.Warm contact path: Public club contact; propose a peer event with ETH robotics students and a 42AI demonstration.

fields.What they build: Makerspace offering fabrication, 3D printing, electronics and CNC workshops. Live site advertises 2026 maker activities; distinct from the Bitwäscherei collective.
fields.Warm contact path: Use public workshop/visitor channels; arrange safety induction and machine access before a group visit.

fields.What they build: Venture investor with industrial-tech/robotics exposure: official portfolio lists autonomous inventory-drone company Verity, invested since 2020. Former investiere branding should not become a second row. Size / stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: Public fund contact; propose a Swiss robotics commercialization talk and ask about a portfolio founder introduction.

fields.What they build: Cantonal bank investing in Swiss technology ventures. Venturelab's October 2025 Tethys financing announcement names it among participants in a EUR 3.5M pre-seed round.
fields.Warm contact path: Public startup-finance channel; request an educational founder-financing talk. No existing warm introduction.

fields.What they build: Engineering education program where teams design and build prototypes over fifth/sixth semesters, including robotics and medical/mobility systems; results presented at Focus Rollout. Program row, not a duplicate of each participating club or RSL.
fields.Warm contact path: Ask the department's public education/event contact for a robotics focus-team exchange or public rollout visit.

fields.What they build: Builds collaborative arms and mobile manipulators including Lio and Sola for care, research and laboratory workflows. Official contact address is Rohrstrasse 36, Glattbrugg. Size / stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: Public company contact; propose a manipulation/teleoperation engineering talk with a small SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Laboratory automation company. Fluent workstations combine pipetting robotic arms with gripper arms for moving plates and labware; this is tangible robotics, not just diagnostic software.
fields.Warm contact path: Public automation/application contact; request a lab-automation engineering talk or a nonclinical workflow case study.

fields.What they build: Dynamic measurement company supplying force, torque, pressure and acceleration sensors. 9306A measures six-axis forces/moments; relevant to contact measurement and robot testing, not an entire robot platform.
fields.Warm contact path: Public technical contact for an educational force-measurement session; ask for application advice before hardware support.

fields.What they build: Elios 3 collision-tolerant confined-space inspection drones reduce human entry into hazardous assets; official site also lists ultrasonic-testing payload and tether power options. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: info@flyability.com; request an indoor-inspection/perception engineering talk, not unsupervised industrial flight access.

fields.What they build: ARA620 ultra-high-precision sprayer uses AI to distinguish plants and target treatment. It is a tractor-mounted precision implement, not a claim that all current products are autonomous weeding vehicles. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: Public company contact; propose an agricultural computer-vision discussion or dataset evaluation exercise.

fields.What they build: DEXTER robotic surgery system supports minimally invasive procedures while fitting existing operating-room workflows and instrument preferences. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: info@distalmotion.com; ask for an educational surgical-robotics/systems-safety talk, without requesting patient or operating-room access.

fields.What they build: Emovo Clinic is a robotic hand exoskeleton; Emovo Research offers research-only hand exoskeletons with one to five active fingers, sensing and software APIs. Distinguishes certified clinical and noncertified research devices. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: hello@emovocare.com; request a research API or assistive-manipulation seminar, not clinical testing.

fields.What they build: Develops personal lower-limb exoskeletons to help people with spinal cord injuries stand and walk; emphasizes lightweight user-centered mobility. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: Public company contact for an assistive-robotics design talk. No patient trials or unsupervised exoskeleton use proposed.

nodes.name: EPFL Learning Algorithms and Systems Laboratory (LASA)

fields.What they build: Aude Billard's laboratory studies teaching robots dexterous skills from human demonstrations and adaptive/reactive control under obstacles or perturbations.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official lab/center contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

nodes.name: EPFL Computational Robot Design & Fabrication Lab (CREATE)

fields.What they build: Josie Hughes's laboratory develops computational design and fabrication for sensorized, multi-material robots, manipulation and robot-driven physical experimentation.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official lab/center contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Dario Floreano's group studies bio-inspired aerial, wearable and soft robotics, including drone learning/control and resilient robot design.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official lab/center contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Jamie Paik's laboratory develops reconfigurable, origami and soft robots, novel actuation and wearable interfaces; projects include Tribot, Mori and Mori3.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official lab/center contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Auke Ijspeert's lab studies locomotion, sensorimotor coordination and learning through neuromechanical simulation, amphibious/legged robots and rehabilitation exoskeletons.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official lab/center contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Develops neurotechnologies to restore sensorimotor function. Robotics-relevant work includes sensory prosthetics and cognitive control of an extra robotic arm; not every neuroengineering project is a robot.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official lab/center contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Herbert Shea's laboratory develops compliant actuators, stretchable sensors, soft transducers and wearable haptic displays for applications including soft robotics and dexterous manipulation. Located at EPFL's Neuchâtel site, not Lausanne.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official lab/center contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Technical university providing robotics education, research laboratories, student MAKE projects and spin-off pathways. Separate lab rows identify practical contacts, not additional universities.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official robotics education contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Interfaculty center connecting robotics research, education, students, spin-offs and industrial partners across perception, control, learning, medical robotics and design.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official lab/center contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Student-run EPFL robotics club and makerspace with electronics/mechanical tools, workshops and open sessions. Official page welcomes members from EPFL or other schools; visitor conditions should still be checked.
fields.Warm contact path: robopoly@epfl.ch; arrange a peer build session or introductory workshop visit, checking external access first.

fields.What they build: Student association designs Mars-style rovers and drones for the European Rover Challenge, conducts space-robotics research and teaches robotics through mini-rover projects.
fields.Warm contact path: Public student-team contact; propose a 42AI rover/perception software exchange with a small demo.

fields.What they build: Innovation campus and startup community with coworking/prototyping ecosystem around EPFL; official locations page explicitly includes robotics among represented technologies. Not a stand-alone robotics lab.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official community/park contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Builds EXRAY underwater inspection robots, LUMA optical underwater communications and DISKDRIVE propulsion; aims to acquire asset-integrity data without conventional tethered interventions. Funding stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official company contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Supplies Autonomous Navigation Technology (ANT) and integration support for AGVs, autonomous forklifts and AMRs; focuses on natural-feature navigation rather than building every customer vehicle. Size / stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: No established warm introduction. Use the official company contact to propose a short student technical exchange, sharing a LeRobot/SO-101 demo.

fields.What they build: Develops Webots open-source robot simulator and supplies commercial support, training, consulting and custom robotics simulations. Established simulation publisher, not a new robot-hardware startup. Size / stage: unknown. Official company contact address is Gollion, near Lausanne.
fields.Warm contact path: Public Webots repository/community first; sales@cyberbotics.com for scoped training or simulation advice.

fields.What they build: Human-centered robot learning from a few demonstrations and interactions, including manipulation, optimal control, reinforcement learning and physical human-robot collaboration.
fields.Warm contact path: Public group contact; ask Sylvain Calinon's team for an open-code study discussion and share a small imitation-learning reproduction.

fields.What they build: Applied research/technology-transfer organization developing sensors, intelligent automation and inspection; lab-automation work explicitly combines robotics, imaging, liquid handling and software.
fields.Warm contact path: Public industry/research contact; request an educational sensor-fusion or laboratory-automation talk with a scoped demo.

fields.What they build: Joint USI-SUPSI institute's autonomous robotics area studies self-supervised perception, flying/ground robots, industrial robotics and energy-efficient embedded AI.
fields.Warm contact path: Alessandro Giusti's public SUPSI research contact; propose reproducing an open robotic-perception baseline.

fields.What they build: Applied research lab for collaborative, industrial and mobile robotics, image processing and mechatronics. Advertises practical demonstrations and a robot park including Panda, UR3, P-Rob and Meca500.
fields.Warm contact path: Public laboratory contacts Gabriel Gruener / Raphael Rätz; ask for an educational visit or collaborative-robot safety discussion.

fields.What they build: Applied institute combining robotics, mechatronics and industrial electronics. Robotics expertise includes ROS/ROS 2, mobile manipulation, safety and simulation with RoboDK.
fields.Warm contact path: Public iAi direction/contact; propose a French-language ROS 2 and manipulation software exchange.

fields.What they build: Builds and tests automated machines for manufacturing, mobility, space and medical partners. Teaching/research robot cells include ABB IRB1200, YuMi and KUKA iiwa with vision and force sensing.
fields.Warm contact path: Public robotics laboratory contacts Michel Lauria / Jeremy Olivier; request a French-language student exchange or simulation session.

fields.What they build: Applied institute for modern control, industrial/building automation and mechatronics. Its robotics laboratory supports prototyping, student projects and external access by arrangement; work includes AI weed control.
fields.Warm contact path: Robot-lab contact Wolfgang Fischer; ask for a student demonstration exchange, checking access and fees first.

fields.What they build: Competence Center Mechanical Systems robotics activity develops industrial automation and mobile robots for changing environments, including human-facing tasks, agricultural and care applications.
fields.Warm contact path: Public competence-center contact on the official robotics page; request a short applied autonomy/robot safety exchange.

nodes.name: OST Institute for Lab Automation and Mechatronics (ILT)

fields.What they build: Develops industrial/collaborative robotic solutions, mobile manipulation, lab automation and flexible smart-factory systems.
fields.Warm contact path: ilt@ost.ch or public institute lead Agathe Koller; request an educational mobile-manipulation case study.

fields.What they build: Swiss industrial automation company building robot linear tracks, modular linear axes/gantries, gearboxes, guideways and integrated automation solutions.
fields.Warm contact path: Public technical contact; propose a motion-system and automation-design seminar before considering equipment sponsorship.

fields.What they build: Swiss Hamilton operation develops/manufactures laboratory automation products; liquid-handling robot platforms integrate pipetting, monitoring, consumables and devices for repeatable assay workflows. Parent also operates in the US.
fields.Warm contact path: Public automation/application contact for a nonclinical lab-robot workflow seminar; no established warm introduction.

fields.What they build: Elevator/escalator group using R.I.S.E (Robotic Installation System for Elevators) to drill precise holes and set anchors in elevator shafts. Official historical report describes relieving installers of strenuous repetitive work.
fields.Warm contact path: Public innovation/media contact; ask for a technical construction-robotics case-study talk, not an active-site visit.

fields.What they build: National robotics association launched in 2024, building on the legacy of NCCR Robotics and the Innosuisse-powered Robotics Innovation Booster; connects research, industry and public outreach.
fields.Warm contact path: contact@swiss-robotics.org; ask for student-friendly events and French-speaking research/industry introductions.

fields.What they build: Swiss innovation agency funding research-to-market collaboration, startups and innovation programs. Funder classification, not an equity VC; EPFL LASA explicitly lists its Robotics Innovation Booster.
fields.Warm contact path: Public program information and a Swiss research partner first; ask about eligibility, not a direct grant for a French student club.

nodes.name: AMLD Intelligence Summit (Applied Machine Learning Days)

fields.What they build: EPFL-linked applied-AI event. Organizer's February 2026 announcement lists a live physical-intelligence keynote with EPFL/ETH construction, manipulation and legged robots; wider event is not exclusively robotics.
fields.Warm contact path: Public event organizer channel; inquire about student rates and a small robotics demo or community exchange. Next edition arrangements unknown.

fields.What they build: Student-run EPFL hackathon plus workshops and bootcamps. The 21–22 November 2026 edition is general-purpose, not a verified robotics-only hackathon; suitable for a software/simulation demo with organizer approval.
fields.Warm contact path: Public organizing-team channel; ask if a robot/simulation demo fits event rules. The site says 2026 applications are closed; next-edition availability unknown.

fields.What they build: Open-source project contributor/user community around Webots, hosted in Cyberbotics' public repository with issues, discussions, chat and contribution documentation. Community row is distinct from Cyberbotics' commercial support operation, not a separate incorporated company. Formal size / stage: unknown.
fields.Warm contact path: Start with public GitHub discussions/issues and a minimal reproducible simulation; make a small documentation or model contribution before requesting a speaker.

fields.What they build: Bio-Inspired Robots for Medicine Laboratory develops surgical robotic/mechatronic prototypes, force sensing, telemanipulation, haptic training and rehabilitation systems. University of Basel affiliation; physical lab is in Allschwil (Basel-Landschaft).
fields.Warm contact path: Public lab leads Georg Rauter / Nicolas Gerig; propose a student teleoperation/haptics seminar, with no clinical deployment request.

fields.What they build: Nonprofit association producing and supporting Thymio open-source educational robots designed with EPFL and ECAL. Its current site announces Thymio 3 for September 2026 and offers robotics/STEAM learning resources.
fields.Warm contact path: info@mobsya.org; propose an introductory robotics/outreach workshop or educational-resource contribution.

fields.What they build: Student-led hackathon integrated with START Summit. Official page advertises the next flagship event on 17–19 March 2027 in St. Gallen; industry cases are broader than robotics.
fields.Warm contact path: Public organizing-team contact; ask whether a robotics/simulation prototype is suitable and check student eligibility and equipment rules.

fields.What they build: Startup/investor networking summit; official next edition is 18–19 March 2027 in St. Gallen. General technology event, not a robotics-only conference.
fields.Warm contact path: Public community/event contact; ask about student access and a small robotics demo rather than assuming investor meetings.

fields.What they build: Regional hackathon bringing developers, designers and technology enthusiasts together to prototype industry/community challenges. Robotics-specific challenges were not established.
fields.Warm contact path: Public organizer contact; propose a software/simulation challenge and confirm hardware suitability, next dates and travel costs.

fields.What they build: Nonprofit Geneva-area hackerspace with electronics, wood and metal workshops, 3D printers, CNC tools, soldering and measurement equipment. Official address is in Carouge, not central Geneva.
fields.Warm contact path: comite@posttenebraslab.ch; arrange a Tuesday-evening visit and a small robotics/electronics build exchange.

fields.What they build: Community-operated hackerspace near Lausanne. Current site documents an October 2026 relaunch after an activity pause and a November open-source home-automation community event.
fields.Warm contact path: Public chat/calendar and visitor channels; arrange a French-language build session and check actual opening status.

fields.What they build: Noncommercial association-run makerspace for learning by fabrication and sharing rapid-prototyping tools. Shares the Closel 3 building/address with other maker activity; distinct association branding from FIXME.
fields.Warm contact path: info@fablab-renens.ch; ask about induction, machine bookings and a small SO-101 part-fabrication workshop.

fields.What they build: Digital-fabrication makerspace operated as a project of 89grad GmbH, rather than assuming a nonprofit association. Official contact page describes a Bern workshop connecting engineers and makers.
fields.Warm contact path: info@fablab-bern.ch; ask about visitor access, machine training and paid workshop conditions.

fields.What they build: Association-run makerspace/hackerspace offering 3D printing, CNC machining and laser fabrication. Current official address is Gasstrasse 20, Basel, superseding an older directory address.
fields.Warm contact path: Official Signal group or advertised open evenings; propose a peer electronics/mechanics build session and confirm machine induction.

fields.What they build: National research network developing control/automation theory, industrial demonstrators and responsible/sustainable automation. Current site includes rail energy-efficiency transfer with ETH/FHNW; broader than robotics alone.
fields.Warm contact path: contact@nccr-automation.ch; ask for public control/automation seminars and educational collaborator introductions, not a student-club grant.

fields.What they build: armasuisse/DDPS specialist center researching, testing and transferring unmanned systems for national security and emergency response, including ARCHE disaster-relief assessments. It is a government research/testing unit, not a commercial robot vendor.
fields.Warm contact path: Public center contact for an educational disaster-response robotics/safety presentation; procurement, restricted facilities and military deployment are outside 42AI's scope.

guide.title: Robotics from zero
guide.intro_md:
## What is a robot?
A robot is a machine that senses its surroundings, computes what to do, and acts on the physical world. It may be a wheeled base, a factory arm, a legged machine, or a small desktop companion. A useful mental model is the robot loop: measure → estimate → decide → move → measure again. A webcam provides pixels, a joint encoder provides an angle, and a motor turns an electrical command into torque. A program connects these parts, but the body and environment decide what actions are possible.

A robot differs from a typical web service because its output can move something, contact a person, or fall over. The software must handle uncertain measurements, delays, mechanical limits, and changing surroundings. For example, if an SO-101 arm is told to reach a cube, its software must know the cube's position, translate that target into joint angles, move its servos, and check whether the gripper actually picked the object up. A successful command is not the same as a successful physical action.

## The fields of robotics and how they fit together
Robotics combines several fields into one working system. Mechanisms and actuation define the links, joints, wheels, and motors. Embedded electronics connect computers to sensors and actuators. Sensing measures the world; perception turns camera pixels into objects or marker poses. Kinematics relates joint angles to tool position, while dynamics describes forces and motion. Control chooses motor commands, and planning selects a route or arm trajectory that avoids obstacles.

State estimation combines noisy measurements to estimate where the robot is; simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) estimates position while building a map. Simulation lets a team test a model before using hardware. Robot learning uses demonstrations or interaction data to train policies. Human–robot interaction (HRI) studies how people understand and safely work with robots. No single field solves the task alone. A pick-and-place robot may use an AprilTag for vision, a Kalman filter for position, inverse kinematics for arm angles, PID control for joints, and a learned policy for grasp timing.

## Hardware vs software: what changes when code touches the real world
Robotics software is still software: it uses functions, data structures, tests, logs, and version control. The difference is that its inputs and outputs are connected to noisy, delayed physical devices. A motor can take longer to move under load; a camera can return blurry frames; a wheel can slip. A command may also saturate at a hardware limit. These effects mean that a program that works in a small simulation can fail on the real robot.

Use the same habits you use when debugging a distributed system: timestamp measurements, record versions, make failures observable, and test one component at a time. Add robotics-specific checks too: units, coordinate frames, joint limits, power, and physical clearance. For example, a target written as 0.3 may mean meters, centimeters, or a normalized value; label units at system boundaries. A controller should also report when a sensor is missing instead of silently treating a missing reading as zero.

## How to use these maps
The world map helps you find organizations, robots, projects, and their connections. The Holygraph whiteboard arranges knowledge and projects by branch and learning level, showing prerequisites. Start from a node that looks interesting, read its summary, then open its lesson and resources. Use “start here” as a suggested path, not an exam: if you already understand a prerequisite, move forward. Use groups to collect a team's project stack, and use Guide chat to ask for clarification when it is available.

When following a link, prefer the current official documentation or paper for exact commands and specifications. Blog posts and videos are useful for seeing a system move; they may show an older software version. Write down the device model, firmware, library version, and measurement units before reproducing an example. The map describes relationships, not guaranteed compatibility or support.

## Suggested order
First learn the physical vocabulary: links, joints, actuators, voltage, sensors, and coordinate frames. Next write a small controller in simulation, then use a camera or marker to estimate a target. Learn how a planner converts a target into motion, and how calibration and state estimation handle uncertainty. Only then collect demonstrations or train a robot policy. A practical first chain is: assemble a SO-101 → teleoperate it → record several safe demonstrations → train or run a baseline policy → evaluate on new object positions.

At every step, change one variable and measure the outcome. If the arm misses, check camera calibration, frame transforms, joint calibration, and gripper timing before changing the learned model. Keep the experiment reproducible: save code, data, software version, and a short note about the result. Robotics becomes less mysterious when each physical behavior can be traced through a sensor reading, a computation, and an actuator command.

chapters.title: Mechanisms & actuation: giving a robot a body
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Mechanisms are the links, joints, wheels, gears, belts, and grippers that constrain how a robot can move; an actuator is the device that supplies motion. A LeRobot SO-101 arm makes this visible: six joints move a wrist-mounted gripper, and the follower uses six FEETECH STS3215 servos. Changing link length changes reach and leverage before a line of software is written.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
The mechanism is the physical output stage. A command becomes motor torque, the gears and links turn that torque into movement, and encoders report joint position. A long arm can reach farther but magnifies the load at its shoulder. A wheel that slips can invalidate the controller's assumption that motor rotation equals distance traveled.

## The big ideas
- A **link** is a relatively rigid arm segment, while a **joint** lets two links move relative to each other; the SO-101 shoulder is one example.
- A **gear ratio** of 1:345 means the motor turns 345 times for one output turn, trading speed for torque; friction and backlash make real gears less ideal.
- Geometry sets the workspace: a longer reach raises shoulder torque demand, and joint placement can prevent reaching behind the base. Torque is turning effort; backlash is motion lost when gear teeth change contact after a reversal. Like a software API, the mechanism exposes only motions its structure permits.

## What you'll be able to build
Sketch a two-link arm, mark its joints, identify its motor and gripper, and predict which link sees the largest load. Compare the SO-101's compact tabletop reach with ANYmal's four-legged structure: both are robots, but their mechanisms solve different tasks. Start with actuator sizing and gear trains, then model a part in CAD. Before powering hardware, check that the arm can move through its full range without hitting a table or person.

chapters.title: Embedded & electronics: connecting code to hardware
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Embedded electronics are the circuits and small computers that let software communicate with motors and sensors. A microcontroller reads a command, updates an output pin or bus, and repeats on a fixed schedule. On the SO-101, a host computer talks to FEETECH servos through a serial bus; the motor's control board handles the low-level position loop while LeRobot coordinates the arm.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
The electronic path runs from program to processor, interface, actuator, and sensor feedback. **UART** sends serial bits between devices; **I²C** shares a clocked two-wire bus; **SPI** uses clock and data lines for faster peripheral exchange; **CAN** is a robust multi-node bus used in many mobile robots. The right choice depends on distance, speed, wiring, and fault tolerance.

## The big ideas
- **Voltage** is electrical potential difference, **current** is charge flow, and electrical power is voltage multiplied by current; logic-level pins encode 0 or 1 and cannot power a motor.
- The SO-101's six follower servos share a serial bus but each has an ID, so a command addressed to joint 3 does not need a separate USB cable.
- Bus timing and error replies matter: a **watchdog** can put an actuator into a defined state if its command heartbeat stops. Treat the bus like a network protocol with addresses, packets, and timeouts.

## What you'll be able to build
You will be able to trace a sensor wire to a processor and explain where motor power enters the circuit. Start with the LeRobot wiring and setup instructions, then read a servo's voltage and protocol limits before connecting it. A concrete debugging test is to send a position request to one servo ID and confirm that the reply reports the expected ID and position; silence suggests power, wiring, baud rate, or ID mismatch.

chapters.title: Sensing: measuring the world
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Sensing turns physical events into numbers a program can use. An encoder reports shaft rotation, an inertial measurement unit (IMU) reports acceleration and angular rate, and a camera reports pixels. The SO-101's joint servos include magnetic encoders, so LeRobot can observe joint positions; a separate webcam can show whether the gripper is over a target.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
Sensors close the loop: a command changes the robot, sensors measure the result, and software updates its next action. Measurements are not the world itself. A camera sees a 2-D projection; an IMU measures motion plus bias and vibration; an encoder measures angle but cannot tell whether a wheel slipped on the floor.

## The big ideas
- **Resolution** is the smallest change a sensor distinguishes, **noise** is random variation, and **bias** is a persistent offset; an encoder, IMU, and camera therefore answer different questions.
- Camera intrinsics describe focal length and optical center, while distortion coefficients model lens bending; calibration estimates these values from checkerboard images.
- A known 0.10 m AprilTag supplies physical corner spacing, letting pose estimation scale image pixels into meters. Sensor output is like an API response with uncertainty, not perfect ground truth.

## What you'll be able to build
Compare encoder, IMU, and camera data by asking what each directly measures and what it only implies. In a webcam calibration, photograph a checkerboard from several angles, estimate the camera matrix, then use that calibration before estimating tag pose. OpenCV's current 4.x ArUco tutorial demonstrates detection and pose estimation; the same ideas apply to AprilTags, but the marker families and APIs are not interchangeable. Record a sensor value with its timestamp and units before using it in a robot loop.

chapters.title: Kinematics & dynamics: describing robot motion
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Kinematics describes motion without asking what forces caused it; dynamics studies the forces and masses that do. A robot arm is a chain of coordinate frames attached to its base, links, and tool. If a camera sees a tag 0.30 m in front of it and the camera is mounted 0.10 m above the arm base, transforming between those frames lets the robot express the tag location relative to its gripper.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
A motion planner may ask the tool to move to a point in the room, but each motor needs a joint angle. **Forward kinematics** maps joint angles to tool pose; **inverse kinematics** searches for joint angles that produce a requested pose. Dynamics then predicts required torque while the links accelerate or hold a load.

## The big ideas
- A **coordinate frame** is an origin plus three axes; a **homogeneous transform** is a 4×4 matrix combining rotation and translation. **Forward kinematics** maps joint values to tool pose; **inverse kinematics** finds joint values for a target pose.
- Worked example: frame B is rotated 90° counter-clockwise and sits 2 m right of frame A. Point B=(1,0,0) rotates to (0,1,0), then translates to A=(2,1,0); reversing the order gives a different result.
- ROS 2 tf2 stores timestamped transforms. Frame labels act like types in software: adding a camera-frame point directly to a map-frame point is a coordinate bug.

## What you'll be able to build
Draw the base, shoulder, elbow, and tool frames on an SO-101, then explain how a target point moves through the chain. Use a 4×4 transform to convert a point by hand, and label both source and destination frames. Start with rigid-body transforms before forward kinematics; it prevents a common mistake—treating a robot's measured joint angle as if it were already a world-space position.

chapters.title: Control: making motors do what you mean
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Control makes a robot follow a target despite disturbances and imperfect models. A motor controller compares desired position with measured position and changes motor effort to reduce the error. On a SO-101 joint, if the target is 30° and the encoder reads 24°, the error is +6°; the controller must move the joint toward the target without overshooting or oscillating.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
A controller runs repeatedly: read sensors, compute an error, choose an output, and send it to an actuator. The **proportional** term reacts to current error, the **integral** term accumulates persistent error, and the **derivative** term reacts to how quickly error changes. This is PID control. Too much gain can make the arm shake; too little makes it sluggish.

## The big ideas
- The **sampling period** is the time between controller updates: a loop designed for 10 ms behaves differently if it actually runs every 100 ms.
- PID combines proportional response to current error, integral response to accumulated error, and derivative response to the error's rate of change; on a 10° error, gain 0.4 gives a proportional output of 4 units before limits.
- Saturation caps an output at the motor limit, while integral windup keeps accumulating error during that cap. Tune gains against the robot's mass, gearing, friction, and load; the loop resembles retry-and-correct software, but its output moves hardware.

## What you'll be able to build
Implement a tiny position loop in simulation before testing a motor. For a target of 10 units and measured value 8, error is 2; with proportional gain 0.4, output is 0.8 before limits. Then add integral action only if a constant load leaves a steady error. The MathWorks Tech Talk visualizes each term; ROS 2 Control documents the controller interface used in real robot stacks.

chapters.title: Simulation: practice in a computed world
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
A robot simulator computes a virtual robot's motion so a team can test ideas before using hardware. A scene contains geometry, mass, joints, contact surfaces, and sensors; a physics engine advances them in small time steps. MuJoCo is used for research and robotics examples, while NVIDIA Isaac Lab builds GPU-accelerated robot-learning environments on Isaac Sim.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
The same loop runs in simulation and on hardware: policy or controller reads simulated sensors, produces actions, and receives the next state. But a simulator is a model, not a photocopy of reality. A gripper that succeeds in a frictionless simulation may fail on a smooth real object. Timing, contact, camera exposure, actuator limits, and noise can create sim-to-real gaps.

## The big ideas
- A **time step** is the interval between physics updates: a 0.02 s step produces 50 updates per simulated second, while 0.01 s produces 100 and costs more computation.
- A **collision shape** approximates solid geometry for contact checks; a detailed visual mesh can use a simple box or capsule for faster simulation. Validate units, mass, joint limits, and friction.
- Simulation is a test double: **contact** is where bodies touch and exchange forces, while **model fidelity** describes how closely its assumptions match the real robot. A passing result for an SO-101 in MuJoCo or Isaac Lab is evidence about that setup, not proof about the physical arm.

## What you'll be able to build
Start with a one-joint pendulum or an arm moving a cube, then compare the same trajectory in MuJoCo and Isaac Lab. The Isaac Lab installation tutorial shows a real workflow: launch an example task and observe simulated agents learning locomotion. Record the simulator version, time step, and random seed so another student can reproduce the run. Add sensor noise and imperfect friction before judging whether a learned policy is robust.

chapters.title: Perception: turning sensor data into meaning
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Perception turns sensor measurements into useful descriptions of objects and places. A camera gives an image; a perception program may report “AprilTag ID 7 is 0.6 m ahead, rotated 10°.” The estimate depends on camera calibration, image quality, and the geometry encoded in the marker. A robot can then align its gripper or estimate its location relative to a known tag.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
Perception sits between raw sensing and decisions. The camera driver returns pixels; the detector finds corners and decodes the marker; pose estimation converts corners to a 3-D transform; planning or control consumes that transform. An undetected tag is not the same as a tag at the origin, so software must distinguish “no detection” from a valid zero-valued measurement.

## The big ideas
- A **fiducial marker** is a designed visual pattern with an identity; a **dictionary** is the set of marker codes a detector searches. AprilTag and ArUco are related square-marker families, but their libraries differ.
- OpenCV 4.13.0's ArUco pipeline finds candidate squares, decodes an ID, then estimates **pose**—position and orientation—from the detected corners. Each stage can fail for blur, occlusion, or a wrong dictionary.
- **Camera intrinsics** are focal lengths and optical center; with them and a known 0.10 m tag edge, pixel corners can be scaled to distance in meters. Perception resembles parsing a message: locate, validate, then attach a confidence and frame.

## What you'll be able to build
Print a tag, place it in front of a calibrated webcam, and display its ID and corner locations. For example, use a known 0.10 m marker and a calibrated camera; pose estimation can then distinguish a small nearby tag from the same-sized tag far away. Use OpenCV's 4.x API rather than the obsolete 4.0.1 calibration page, and record the camera model and tag family with the result.

chapters.title: State estimation & SLAM: knowing where the robot is
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
State estimation combines imperfect sensor readings into a best estimate of what a robot is doing. A mobile robot may use wheel encoders for motion, an IMU for rotation, and a camera or GPS for position. **SLAM** means simultaneous localization and mapping: estimate the robot's location while building a map of an unknown environment.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
Sensors supply measurements; an estimator turns them into a time-stamped state; planning uses that state to choose a route. Wheel odometry drifts because small wheel errors accumulate. A camera may correct that drift when it recognizes a landmark. A Kalman filter is one way to combine a prediction with a new, noisy measurement while tracking uncertainty.

## The big ideas
- Worked 1-D Kalman example: the **state estimate** is position; predict 10 m with variance 4 m² (uncertainty), while GPS measures 12 m with variance 1 m². **Kalman gain** = 4/(4+1)=0.8, so the estimate becomes 10+0.8(12−10)=11.6 m and variance becomes 0.8 m².
- The filter weights the more precise GPS reading more, but keeps the motion prediction. Wheel odometry, an IMU, and camera landmarks can play the same complementary roles on a mobile robot.
- **SLAM** estimates location while building a map. An estimator is like merging timestamped logs with confidence: the newest value is not automatically best, and clocks and coordinate frames must agree.

## What you'll be able to build
Plot predicted and corrected position on a line, then add noisy wheel and GPS samples. Inspect how uncertainty shrinks after a reliable measurement and grows while the robot moves without observations. The ROS `robot_localization` package applies these ideas to robot messages, while the Python book makes the update equations runnable. Do not call the result “ground truth”: it is an estimate with assumptions and uncertainty.

chapters.title: Planning: choosing a route or motion
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Planning chooses a sequence of safe motions from a start to a goal. A mobile robot may need a route through corridors; an arm may need a collision-free joint path to a cup. The map or robot geometry defines which motions are possible, while obstacles rule out others. Planning often returns a path; a controller still has to track it.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
A perception system supplies obstacles and robot pose, a planner searches for a route or trajectory, and a controller turns that plan into wheel or joint commands. In ROS 2, Nav2 handles mobile navigation tasks; MoveIt plans arm motion. The planner's output depends on the map, robot footprint, joint limits, and collision model, so a stale map can invalidate an otherwise good path.

## The big ideas
- A **configuration** is a robot pose or joint-angle vector; configuration space treats every possible configuration as a point and marks collisions as forbidden.
- On a grid, if a wall blocks the direct cell from (0,0) to (2,0), A* (A-star), a grid search that always expands the cell with the lowest cost-so-far plus estimated distance to the goal, can route around it through (0,1), (1,1), and (2,1); RRT instead grows a tree by sampling configurations, which suits high-dimensional arms.
- A planner returns a proposed path, not motor commands. Like a route-finding service, it needs a valid map and constraints; a controller still applies timing and velocity limits before execution.

## What you'll be able to build
Create a 2-D grid with a rectangular obstacle, run A* (A-star), and compare the result with a straight-line route that collides. Then use a simulator or Nav2 to plan a path for a differential-drive robot. On an arm, inspect MoveIt's collision scene and plan a grasp approach. Start with a small deterministic map before debugging a full sensor-driven environment.

chapters.title: Manipulation: reaching, grasping, and moving objects
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Manipulation is using a robot arm, hand, or gripper to change the world. Pick-and-place sounds simple—reach, grasp, lift, move, release—but each step depends on geometry, force, contact, and uncertainty. The SO-101 has a parallel gripper at the end of a six-joint arm; ALOHA uses two low-cost arms to collect demonstrations for bimanual tasks.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
A manipulation pipeline estimates an object's pose, chooses a grasp, plans an approach, closes the gripper, checks whether the object moved, and then plans a transfer. A pose estimate that is off by 2 cm may cause a narrow gripper to miss. Tactile or motor-current feedback can help detect contact, but a basic setup may use camera images and joint positions only.

## The big ideas
- The SO-101's six-joint arm ends in a parallel gripper; ALOHA uses two arms for bimanual work. A **grasp** is a contact arrangement that holds an object, and workspace is where the tool can reach.
- A **trajectory** is a timed sequence of positions. A 2 cm error in an object's pose can make a narrow gripper miss; plan a clear approach, align, close, check contact, then lift and verify that the object moved.
- **Contact force** is the push exchanged where surfaces touch; stable contact must balance weight and disturbance. Manipulation is like a transaction: observe, attempt, verify, then commit the transfer—or recover instead of reporting success.

## What you'll be able to build
Start with a cube on a table and teleoperate the SO-101 to pick it up. Use a fixed camera and mark the object's center; record each attempt so misses become diagnosable. ALOHA's ACT work used action chunks to perform tasks such as bimanual manipulation, while LeRobot provides a current recording and rollout workflow. Keep objects lightweight and keep hands out of the arm's path during powered tests.

chapters.title: Locomotion: moving through the world
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about
Locomotion is how a robot moves its body through the world. Wheeled bases roll; legged robots alternate contact between feet; tracked robots distribute force over a belt. ETH Zurich's ANYmal is a quadruped designed for rough industrial environments. Its legs can step over uneven ground where a small differential-drive robot would get stuck.

## Where it sits in the robot loop
The robot estimates its body motion, selects foot placements or wheel speeds, and controls joints or motors while the ground pushes back. A gait is a repeating pattern of contacts and swings. An IMU estimates body orientation; joint encoders report leg configuration; foot contact sensors can reveal whether a planned step actually landed.

## The big ideas
- Wheeled bases roll, tracked robots spread force over a belt, and legged robots use a **gait**, a repeating contact pattern; ETH Zurich's ANYmal is a quadruped built for rough terrain.
- **Stance** is when a foot supports the body; **swing** is when it moves without ground support. Faster motion needs timed foot placement and center-of-mass control for **dynamic stability**, balance maintained through motion and momentum.
- Each foot alternates between support and flight like a service that is sometimes available and sometimes disconnected. The controller coordinates those phases using body orientation, joint encoders, and contact feedback.

## What you'll be able to build
Plot a gait timeline for a slow quadruped, showing stance and swing for each leg. Then compare it with a two-wheeled robot that turns by setting left and right wheel speeds. ETH RSL's ANYmal videos make the terrain challenge concrete; the open `rsl_rl` project shows how reinforcement learning can train legged policies. Begin in simulation and measure body tilt and foot slip before judging a gait by appearance alone.
